ru.title: How to play (for beginners)
ru.short: Learn to draw lines, take boxes and win by trying it on small boards (about 2 minutes)
ru.p1.t: Join two dots with a line
ru.p1.b:
The board is a grid of dots. Two players take turns, one line each, joining two neighbouring dots horizontally or vertically. Diagonals are not allowed.

The first player is red, the second blue. Watch red and blue take turns on the board below.
ru.p1.task: Draw any line you like (tap the board).
ru.p1.ok: That's it! You may draw anywhere — but which line you choose decides the game.
ru.p2.t: Draw the fourth side to take a box
ru.p2.b:
Whoever draws the fourth and last side of a small square (a box) takes it. The box gets your colour and is worth one point.

Boxes with three sides drawn glow with a dotted frame.
ru.p2.task: One box has three sides. Draw the fourth side and take it.
ru.p2.ok: Got it! The box is yours — one point.
ru.p2.ng: That line does not finish a box. Draw the missing side of the glowing box.
ru.p3.b:
After taking a box you must draw another line. So a row of connected boxes can be taken one after another.

Your turn ends when you draw a line that does not take a box.
ru.p3.task: Take all three connected boxes in a row.
ru.p3.more: Box {n}! You move again — keep going.
ru.p3.ok: All three! Because every box gives you another move, connected boxes are taken in one go.
ru.p3.ng: That line takes no box, so your turn would end. Draw the fourth side of the glowing box.
ru.p4.b:
If you draw the third side of a box, your opponent draws the fourth and takes it. Drawing a third side is a present for your opponent.

A line that gives no box a third side is called a safe line. As a beginner, choose safe lines.
ru.p4.task: Draw a safe line that gives no box away.
ru.p4.ok: Correct! No box has three sides. That is a safe line.
ru.p4.ng: That line gives a box three sides, and your opponent (blue) takes it. Try again.
ru.p5.t: Score and end of the game
ru.p5.b:
When every line is drawn (every box is taken) the game ends. Whoever has more boxes wins.

On boards with an even number of boxes (4×4 has 16) an 8–8 draw is possible. Watch blue draw the last lines in a row below.
ru.p5.task: The game ends with the last line.
ru.p5.ok: All lines are drawn. Red {a} – {b} Blue: blue wins.
ru.p6.b:
Boards are named by their number of boxes. “3×3” means 3×3 = 9 boxes (and 4×4 = 16 dots).

3×3 takes a few minutes and suits beginners, 4×4 is the standard size, 5×5 is a long and deep game. Start with 3×3.
ru.p7.b:
That is all the rules. In short:

① take turns drawing one line ② draw a box's fourth side to take it ③ after taking a box, move again ④ more boxes wins

The secrets of strong play: don't hand out third sides, and when you must give boxes away, give as few as possible. The lessons then teach the expert ideas — chains, double-dealing and the long chain rule — step by step.
course.basic.sub: Safe lines, the third side, taking boxes, chains and loops. Start here once you know the rules.
course.mid.sub: Handing out 2-chains, double-dealing, control, the long chain rule and sacrifices — the core ideas of winning.
course.adv.sub: Loops and chains in the endgame, counting the endgame, and plans for the 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 opening and middlegame.
course.exam.sub: Questions from every topic, the harder positions of each board.
ls.desc2: After the rules, 15 steps teach how to win. Each step has an explanation and 5 problems (20 points each, rank-based scoring, pass with 75). Every problem and answer was checked by the exact solver.
ls.examNote: Final problems: hints are text only.
ls.firstNote: Problem 1 uses the same idea as the worked example. Stuck? “Hint” shows helpers on the board.
ls.scoring: Scoring: the best move scores 20. Other moves score less step by step, ranked by the final result they lead to. 75 points or more out of 100 passes.
ls.exampleCap: Example: the gold line is correct (with best play: you {a} – {b} opponent).
ls.alsoBest: This position has {n} best moves, all with the same result.
ls.aidSafe: Green dotted = safe lines ({n} now). Long chains (3+ boxes): {l}.
ls.aidChain: Numbers = length of the chain each box belongs to (L = loop).
ls.needPass: You need 75 points to pass. Try again.
ls.graduate: 🎓 Congratulations, you graduated! Keep sharpening your play with the puzzles and the strong AI.
r.shouldDecline: Here the right idea was not to take everything but to leave the last two boxes (four in a loop) and pass the turn.
r.shouldTake: Here you should take every box. Leaving boxes simply hands them to your opponent.
r.declineOk: You left boxes and made your opponent open the next chain.
r.takeOk: Taking everything is right: the boxes in front of you are worth more than keeping control.
r.missedTake: You drew elsewhere without taking the box, so your opponent gets it.
r.gaveBoxes: This line gives a third side and hands {n} box(es) to your opponent.
r.sacOk: A deliberate sacrifice of {n} box(es) that wins control.
r.afterBest: / after the best move {m}: {s} safe lines, {l} long chains
r.comps: Chains and loops on the board: {c}
ls.chain.fig: Chains and loops: the four boxes top left form a loop (L4); the five boxes around it are one long chain.
ls.double.fig: Your opponent opened a chain. After taking two boxes, leave the last two and draw the gold line at the end: your opponent gets two boxes but must open the next chain.
ls.safe.d: Find lines that give no box a third side
ls.safe.body: Whoever draws a box's fourth side takes it. So drawing a third side gives a box to your opponent.
A line that gives no box a third side is a safe line. In the opening and middlegame both players draw safe lines. Remember: the sides of a box that already has two lines are dangerous.
ls.safe.q: Draw a line that gives your opponent no box.
ls.safe.hint: Look for a line that touches no box with two lines already.
ls.safe.tip: While safe lines remain, use them first. Later you will see that the number of safe lines also decides the game.
ls.safe.ex: The green dotted lines are safe too and lead to the same result.
ls.third.d: Spot the lines that give boxes away on 4×4
ls.third.body: On bigger boards two-sided boxes appear everywhere and it gets easy to draw a third side by accident.
An inner line touches two boxes. Even if one side is safe, the other may already have two lines. Lines on the edge touch only one box. Make it a habit to count both boxes of a line.
ls.third.q: Draw a line that gives no box away.
ls.third.hint: Check the boxes on both sides of the line. If either has two lines, you give it a third.
ls.third.tip: An inner line changes two boxes at once. Checking both sides prevents careless losses.
ls.take.d: Take what you can, then think about the next line
ls.take.body: A box with three sides is yours with the fourth line. Since you move again afterwards, take first and then choose your next line — it costs nothing.
If you ignore a box you could take and draw elsewhere, your opponent takes it and gets the move as well. Boxes glowing with a dotted frame can be taken now.
ls.take.q: A box can be taken. Draw the best line.
ls.take.hint: Where is the missing side of the glowing (three-sided) box?
ls.take.tip: Missing a free box usually costs two: the one your opponent takes and the one you didn't.
ls.chain.d: When safe lines run out, hand over the smallest chain
ls.chain.body: When no safe line is left, every line gives boxes away. The board has split into rows of connected boxes — chains — and rings — loops.

Drawing any line in a chain lets your opponent take the whole chain. So give the shortest chain first. Chains of three or more boxes are long chains; whoever has to open the first long chain usually loses.
The hint shows on each box the length of its chain (L for loops).
ls.chain.q: Every line gives boxes away. Draw the line that loses least.
ls.chain.hint: The numbers are chain lengths. Which chain is the smallest?
ls.chain.tip: Hand out chains from the smallest up. Whatever line you open it with, the whole chain goes to your opponent.
ls.hard.d: Open a two-box chain in the middle
ls.hard.body: If you open a two-box chain with an end line, your opponent can decline the two boxes by drawing the line beyond them and push the turn back to you.
Open it with the middle line and the two boxes become two separate single boxes: your opponent can only take them (if not, you take them yourself). This hand-out gives your opponent no control.
ls.hard.q: You must hand out a two-box chain. Draw the best line.
ls.hard.hint: Which line of the 2-chain leaves your opponent no way to hand it back?
ls.hard.tip: Two-box chains from the middle. Opening at the end gives your opponent a choice (take or decline).
ls.double.d: Leave the last two boxes of a long chain to keep control
ls.double.body: When your opponent opens a long chain you want to take it all. But then you must open the next chain yourself.
Instead, leave the last two boxes and draw the line beyond them to end your turn (double-dealing). Your opponent takes both boxes with one line (a double-cross) and then has to open the next chain.
That is how you keep control: two boxes now, the next long chain later.
ls.double.q: Two boxes of the chain your opponent opened are left. Draw the best line.
ls.double.hint: If you take everything, who opens the next chain? To leave two, which line do you draw?
ls.double.tip: All-but-two is the standard technique while another long chain remains. If the rest is big enough, the two boxes come back quickly.
ls.control.d: Decide by counting what control is worth
ls.control.body: Leaving two (four in a loop) is not always right: each time you hand over two (four) boxes.
If the remaining chains are small, or this is the last chain, take everything. If a big long chain remains, leave boxes and keep control.
Rule of thumb: compare the boxes you give by leaving with the boxes you gain later by keeping control.
ls.control.q: Boxes can be taken. Take them all, or leave some? Draw the best line.
ls.control.hint: Count the remaining chains. Will the next long chain repay the boxes you give?
ls.control.tip: Control is worth as much as the remaining long chains. When they are small, just take.
ls.parity.d: The parity of long chains decides who gets control
ls.parity.body: When the safe lines run out, whoever must open the first long chain usually loses. Who that is depends on the parity of the number of moves.

Berlekamp's long chain rule: count the dots of the board. The first player wants dots + long chains to be even, the second player wants it odd. On 3×3 (16 dots) the first player wants an even number of long chains; on 4×4 (25 dots) an odd number.
Choose your safe lines to join or split chains and steer the number of long chains to your parity.
ls.parity.q: Safe lines remain, but they are not all equal. Think about the long chains and draw the best line.
ls.parity.hint: Does this line join chains or split them? How many long chains will there be?
ls.parity.tip: Which safe line you draw shapes the chains. Matching the number of long chains to your parity is the middlegame goal.
ls.parity.ex: The other safe lines (green) leave a long-chain parity that favours your opponent.
ls.sacrifice.d: Give boxes on purpose to flip the parity
ls.sacrifice.body: The side losing the long chain fight can flip the parity by giving away one or two boxes on purpose, even while safe lines remain.
Give a little to win a lot: who takes the last long chain matters far more than one box now.
ls.sacrifice.q: Safe lines exist, but they lose. Draw the best line.
ls.sacrifice.hint: If both sides draw safe lines, who opens the long chain at the end? Can a small sacrifice change that?
ls.sacrifice.tip: A sacrifice buys control of the long chains. The fewer boxes you give and the bigger the chains, the better.
ls.sacrifice.ex: After a green safe line you would be the one forced to open a long chain.
ls.loop.t: Loops and chains in the endgame
ls.loop.d: All but four in a loop — and the order matters
ls.loop.body: To keep control in an opened loop, leave the last four boxes and draw the middle line, handing over two pairs. A loop costs four boxes, not two.
So the side without control opens loops first to make the controller pay four boxes. Decide from the sizes left whether to open chains or loops first, and whether to leave or take.
ls.loop.q: An endgame with a loop. Draw the best line.
ls.loop.hint: Leaving boxes in a loop costs four. Can the remaining chains pay that back?
ls.loop.tip: Loops are expensive for the controller. Without control, open loops first and wear your opponent down.
ls.count.d: Work out the order of chains from their sizes
ls.count.body: Once safe lines are gone, the board is a set of chains and loops. The controller leaves two (four in loops) on every chain but the last; the other side chooses an order that loses least.
How to count: the controller's share is all boxes minus two per kept chain (four per loop). Many small chains (1–2 boxes) lower the value of control. Try different orders to find the best opening.
ls.count.q: No safe line is left. Count the order of chains and draw the best line.
ls.count.hint: Who has control? What happens if you open the loop first?
ls.count.tip: The endgame is arithmetic: count the chains and add up what leaving and taking gain.
ls.open3.d: The first moves set up the number of long chains
ls.open3.body: 3×3 (16 dots) is solved: with best play the second player wins 6–3. Still, the opening has many positions where one move changes the result.

The first player wants an even number of long chains, the second an odd number. Edges of the centre box and lines that cut the board shape the chains. See also the solver-checked lines in the Openings tab.
ls.open3.q: A 3×3 opening. Draw the best line.
ls.open3.hint: Into what chains will this line split the board? How many long ones?
ls.open3.tip: In the opening, imagine where the long chains will form.
ls.mid4.d: With 25 dots the first player wants an odd number of long chains
ls.mid4.body: 4×4 (25 dots) is a draw, 8–8, with best play. With an odd number of dots the long chain rule says the first player wants an odd number of long chains, the second an even number.
In the middlegame every safe line fixes the chains a little more. Ask which lines join long chains and which split them.
ls.mid4.q: A 4×4 middlegame. Draw the best line.
ls.mid4.hint: Find the long-chain candidates. Does this line join or split them?
ls.mid4.tip: One middlegame line can be worth several endgame boxes. Read the chain shapes ahead.
ls.mid5.d: Count the chains on a big board too
ls.mid5.body: 5×5 (36 dots) is not solved. These problems use only positions with few safe lines left that the solver reads to the end.
36 dots is even, so the first player wants an even number of long chains, the second an odd number. With more chains and loops, taking and leaving are worth more too.
ls.mid5.q: A 5×5 middle- or endgame. Draw the best line.
ls.mid5.hint: Count the safe lines left and the long chains and loops.
ls.mid5.tip: On big boards the count of long chains and loops decides the game.
ls.exam.d: Five harder problems from every topic
ls.exam.body: The last step mixes everything: safe lines, taking and leaving, the long chain rule, sacrifices, loops and endgame counting. Find out which idea each position needs.
ls.exam.q: Find the idea the position needs and draw the best line.
ls.exam.hint: Any safe lines left? Boxes to take? How many long chains and loops?
ls.exam.tip: When unsure: boxes to take → leave or take → parity of safe lines → order of hand-outs.
op.title: Openings (solver-verified lines)
op.desc: Learn the 3×3 and 4×4 openings from lines checked by the exact solver and opening book. Click a line to replay it on the board, step with ◀ ▶, switch lines with ‹ ›. Use ● / ○ to drill the first or second player's side.
op.credit: Dots and Boxes has no traditional opening names like chess or shogi. The names here are descriptive, and every move was verified as optimal by this site's solver (3×3: full search; 4×4: a precomputed exact opening book plus the solver). Background: E. Berlekamp, “The Dots-and-Boxes Game” (long chain rule, double-dealing). The 4×5 board was shown to be a draw by Barker & Korf (AAAI 2012).
op.s3.short: 16 dots. Second player wins 6–3 with best play. Four kinds of first move and the sharp “centre box”
op.s3.intro: 3×3 (16 dots, 24 lines) is solved: with best play the second player wins 6–3 (checked by this site's solver; every one of the 24 first moves gives the same result).

By symmetry there are four kinds of first move: A outer edge at a corner, B outer edge in the middle, C inner line from the border, D side of the centre box. A–C leave the reply open; only a few replies are bad. D is sharp: up to symmetry there are only three best replies.

The key is the long chain rule. With 16 dots the first player wants an even number of long chains, the second an odd number. In most lines below the second player ends up with one long chain and control.

Mirroring (answering with the line point-symmetric about the centre) is no winning recipe. On 3×3 every line has a mirror line, but it is the best move only in about half of the positions. Mirroring the D opening loses a box (“The mirror trap”).
op.s4.short: 25 dots. A draw, 8–8, with best play. One-box traps from early on
op.s4.intro: 4×4 (25 dots, 40 lines) is solved too: best play gives an 8–8 draw (checked by this site's solver and opening book; all 40 first moves draw).

The opening is flexible and most moves keep the draw, but some already lose a box. For example, after the first move b3– (a line touching the centre dot) the eight replies on the right side (c2– d2– c4– d4– d2| e2| d3| e3|) lose a box for the second player.
25 dots is odd, so the first player wants an odd number of long chains, the second an even number. Safe lines last for more than 20 moves: the opening prepares the chain count.

In ● lines (drill as first player) the second player plays the opening book's best moves; in ○ lines (drill as second player) the first player does. In a drill any other optimal move also counts as correct.
op.studyNote: Click a line to replay it on the board. Each position also shows how many moves keep the result — the fewer, the more care it needs.
op.atPly: Move {n} ({who} to play): {k} of {t} moves keep the result.
op.struct: Safe lines ran out after move {k}; the board split into chains {c}. {l} long chain(s) → {d} dots + {l} = {s} ({p}). By the long chain rule that favours the {w} player.
op.noLong: Safe lines ran out after move {k}; the board split into chains {c}. With no long chain, the order of handing out short chains decides the game.
op.loopNote: Loops can change the simple parity count.
op.value3: Value of the start: first player −3 (with best play the second wins 6–3).
op.value4: Value of the start: 0 (best play draws 8–8).
op.drillHint: The gold line is the move of the line (using a hint counts as a miss).
op.drillYour: Your move ({c}). Draw the next move of the line.
op.drillMiss: {m} gives a worse result. The line plays {a}.
op.drillAlt: {m} is also a best move with the same result. The line continues with {a}.
op.N.d1: The first move b2– (a side of the centre box) is sharp. Up to symmetry the second player has three best replies; here a3–, a line from the border inward. Move 6, b2|, is the only best move. The end is one long chain (4 boxes) plus short chains: 16 + 1 is odd and the second player has control.
op.L.d2: Centre box, answered on the far edge
op.N.d2: b2– answered by the opposite outer middle edge b4–. Moves 6 and 8 are again only moves. The end is one 6-box long chain plus a single box — one long chain, odd: the second player's winning pattern.
op.L.d3: Centre box, answered with a vertical line
op.N.d3: b2– answered by the inner vertical b1|. In this line no long chain ever forms; the game becomes a hand-out of one- and two-box chains. Even with short chains only, careful ordering keeps the second player three boxes ahead.
op.N.dx: Answering b2– with its mirror b3– (the opposite side of the centre box) loses a box for the second player (6–3 becomes 5–4). Only 2 of 22 moves keep the gain for the first player, so this line is for drilling the first player.
op.L.a1: Outer corner, answered next to it
op.N.a1: a1– (corner edge) answered by the neighbouring b1–, a quiet line. Moves 4–7 have only one to three best moves each. The end is a 4-box long chain plus two 2-chains: one long chain, second player in control.
op.L.a2: Outer corner, answered at the far corner
op.N.a2: a1– answered by c1– at the other end of the same side. Moves 7–11 are mostly only moves. The end is one 6-box long chain plus a 2-chain.
op.L.a3: Outer corner, answered in the same box
op.N.a3: a1– answered by a1|, the other outer side of the same corner box. The end is a 5-box long chain plus a 2-chain and a single box; the second player takes control.
op.N.b1: b1– (middle of the outer edge) answered by the inner a2–. Moves 4, 6 and 8 are only moves. The end is one 6-box long chain plus a single box.
op.L.b2: Outer middle, answered with a vertical
op.N.b2: b1– answered by the inner vertical b1|. A patient line: for a long time only about two moves keep the result. The end is a 5-box chain, a 2-chain and a single box.
op.L.b3: Outer middle, answered at the centre box
op.N.b3: b1– answered by b3–, the bottom of the centre box. Safe lines last until move 18; the end is one 3-box long chain plus a single box.
op.L.c1: Inner line, answered on a far outer edge
op.N.c1: a2– (a line from the border inward) answered by c1– on the top right edge. The end is a 4-box long chain plus two 2-chains.
op.N.c2: a2– answered by the parallel a3–. Safe lines run out after move 10; the board splits into five chains of 1, 2, 3, 2 and 1 boxes. The only long chain is the 3-chain, and the second player has control.
op.L.c3: Inner line, answered vertically from the same dot
op.N.c3: a2– answered by a2| from the same dot. Safe lines last until move 17; the end is a 4-box long chain plus a single box.
op.L.f9: From the centre dot (book main line)
op.N.f9: The opening book's first move b3– (touching the centre dot c3) and its main line. In the first four moves every move keeps the draw for the first player: the 4×4 opening is forgiving.
op.L.f8: From the edge towards the centre
op.N.f8: Starting with a3– (middle row at the left edge). At move 7, 4 of 34 moves lose a box: from here you must be careful.
op.N.f4: Starting with a2–. At move 7, 8 of 34 moves lose a box — the trickiest of the first-player lines.
op.N.s10: The second player answers b3– with c3–, making a straight line through the centre. At move 8, 11 of 33 moves lose a box: no time to relax.
op.L.s27: A right angle at the centre
op.N.s27: The second player answers b3– with c2|, a vertical line from the centre dot. At move 6, 12 of 35 moves lose: the first critical point.
op.N.s4: The second player answers b3– with a2– at the top left. Moves 4, 6 and 8 each have six to eight losing moves — good drill material.
op.N.s22: The second player answers b3– with c1|. The opening is forgiving, but at move 8 four moves lose.
op.N.s0: The second player answers b3– with the distant corner a1–. At move 2, 8 of 39 replies lose a box, but this line continues fairly calmly.
pc.take.d: Take what you can — positions where taking everything is right
pc.take.long: Boxes are on offer and taking all of them is right. Keep playing best moves after the capture to reach the target score. Levels 1–3 are 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5.
pc.double.d: Leave the last two boxes and pass the turn
pc.double.long: Leave the last two boxes of the chain your opponent opened to keep control. The first move is always the leaving line. Levels 1–3 are 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5.
pc.longchain.d: Pick the one safe line that fixes the parity
pc.longchain.long: Middlegames with safe lines left. Exactly one safe line is correct: it steers the number of long chains to your parity. Levels 1–3 are 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5.
pc.loop.d: All but four, and when to open loops
pc.loop.long: Positions about leaving four in an opened loop or opening loops first. Levels 1–3 are 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5.
pc.sacrifice.d: Skip the safe lines and give boxes on purpose
pc.sacrifice.long: Drawing a safe line loses here. Find the one line that gives boxes away and flips the parity. Levels 1–3 are 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5.
pc.count.d: Work out how to open and hand out chains and loops
pc.count.long: Endgames without safe lines: which chain to open and how (2-chains in the middle, loops first …). When every line of the same chain gives the same result, each of them is correct. Levels 1–3 are 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5.
pc.real3.d: Mixed problems from 3×3 games, theme hidden
pc.real3.long: Positions from 3×3 games with the theme hidden. Exactly one first move is correct. Beginner, intermediate and advanced levels.
pc.real4.long: Positions from 4×4 games with the theme hidden. Exactly one first move is correct. Beginner, intermediate and advanced levels.
pc.real5.d: Read big-board endgames to the end
pc.real5.long: 5×5 endgames, chosen so that the solver reads them completely. Exactly one first move is correct. Beginner, intermediate and advanced levels.
